title: What does the fiscal plan assume?
subtitle: PREFU 2026 tax and expense ratios
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises.

title: A surplus and cash to repay debt are different
subtitle: Operating balances and residual cash
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises.

title: The baseline changed between Budget and the election
subtitle: Same measure and year, two Treasury vintages
interpretation: Revision is not a party's policy saving. Each vintage retains its own actual/forecast labels; the September baseline also changes assumptions.

title: Revenue growth and expense growth both matter
subtitle: 2025/26 to 2030/31 change in the core Crown revenue-minus-expenses balance
interpretation: Nominal accounting decomposition. This is the core Crown balance, not consolidated OBEGALx, and does not identify inflation's causal contribution.

title: Where does forecast spending growth sit?
subtitle: Functional expense changes, 2025/26 to 2030/31
interpretation: Future operating allowances are unallocated, so existing health/education baselines are not the full future service budgets. Nominal figures include prices and demand.

title: Which debt measure is being promised?
subtitle: Three published Treasury definitions on the same chart
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises. The definitions cover different assets and liabilities; a change in definition does not repay debt.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: Tax can rise without a rise in real earnings
subtitle: 2% annual inflation; fixed thresholds versus fully indexed thresholds; current rates in both arms
interpretation: Income-tax arithmetic only: no ACC, tax credits or transfers. This is a household scenario, not aggregate revenue or all Treasury fiscal drag.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: The cost of frozen thresholds depends on inflation
subtitle: Constant real earnings; the same progressive tax schedule throughout
interpretation: Annual endpoint difference, not ten-year cumulative revenue; CPI indexation removes inflation progression, not progression from real wage growth.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: An interest payment is not all purchasing-power income
subtitle: Assumed 5% nominal interest and 33% income-tax rate
interpretation: Indexed comparator deducts inflation compensation from taxable interest, with no refund for negative real returns. Rate is assumed, not a current deposit quote.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: Nominal-interest taxation affects taxpayers differently
subtitle: 5% assumed nominal interest across illustrative tax rates
interpretation: Tax-rate comparisons do not describe the income or wealth distribution. Portfolio taxation has additional rules not modelled here.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: Small differences in annual tax compound
subtitle: $100,000 initial saving; 5% nominal interest; 33% tax; no deposits or withdrawals
interpretation: A deterministic saving illustration; fixed rates and inflation, no fees or investment risk. It is not a retirement or policy revenue forecast.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: How much capital-gains tax comes from inflation?
subtitle: $500,000 eligible property; 28% proposed rate; zero real capital growth
interpretation: Scenario begins at the proposed 1 July 2027 valuation/acquisition date. Zero improvements/costs; family home and other exempt assets excluded. Not a forecast of house prices or receipts.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: A nominal tax rate and a tax on real gains differ
subtitle: 28% of nominal gains; 2% inflation; positive real gains only
interpretation: Undefined when real gains are zero, so those cases are excluded. Capital-only comparison: ignores rental returns, deductions and financing. Indexation also changes revenue and simplicity.

topic: 2. Not taxing inflation and capital gains
title: Why nominal amounts need a price benchmark
subtitle: Observed national CPI; June 2010 purchasing power = 100
interpretation: CPI is a broad consumption benchmark, not each household's inflation and not an asset-price index. Shows price-level accumulation rather than an annual inflation rate.

title: Separate the programmes before discussing welfare savings
subtitle: Major benefit expenses, PREFU 2026
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises. Jobseeker includes health-related recipients and Emergency Benefit; it is not spending solely on unemployed work-ready people.

title: Which benefits drive forecast spending growth?
subtitle: Ten largest absolute changes between 2025/26 and 2030/31
interpretation: Nominal changes combine payment rates, numbers and programme changes. This does not identify a policy saving or imply that programmes serve the same purpose.

title: Two different groups within Jobseeker Support
subtitle: Quarter-end counts from 2008; official backcasts before July 2013
interpretation: Work-ready and health-condition/disability categories do not identify employment status. Some recipients work. Source rounding and classification changes matter.

title: Benefit receipt needs labour-market context
subtitle: HLFS seasonally adjusted rates, 2000 to June 2026
interpretation: Employment rate uses the working-age population; unemployment uses the labour force. Neither is an administrative Jobseeker count. Descriptive context, not causal attribution.

title: Gross benefit reductions are not net fiscal savings
subtitle: 2025/26 unaudited expense base; offsets are assumptions
interpretation: Whole-programme arithmetic, not a work-ready-only cut or party costing. Offsets combine replacement assistance/lost taxes; administration and behavioural responses still excluded.

title: Put the current debate in a longer spending history
subtitle: Treasury actual expenses, 2001-2025; separately dated historical pack
interpretation: Income-replacement basket joins predecessor programmes across reforms. Broad classification is not the work-ready spending base; older vintage differs from restated PREFU values.

title: Cost and appointment availability are separate barriers
subtitle: NZ Health Survey; compare shared years rather than imputing missing observations
interpretation: Survey adults are 15+; year labels name July-June survey periods. Barriers can overlap and must not be added. Ribbons/bars are published 95% confidence intervals.

title: Who faces each access barrier?
subtitle: Adults by age, 2024/25
interpretation: Survey adults are 15+; year labels name July-June survey periods. Barriers can overlap and must not be added. Ribbons/bars are published 95% confidence intervals.

title: Does the access problem follow deprivation?
subtitle: NZDep neighbourhood groups, 2024/25
interpretation: Survey adults are 15+; year labels name July-June survey periods. Barriers can overlap and must not be added. Ribbons/bars are published 95% confidence intervals. Area deprivation is not personal income; these are unadjusted prevalences.

title: Access matters most when need is greater
subtitle: Disabled and non-disabled adults, 2024/25
interpretation: Survey adults are 15+; year labels name July-June survey periods. Barriers can overlap and must not be added. Ribbons/bars are published 95% confidence intervals. Unadjusted comparison; age and need differ.

title: Access barriers differ across population groups
subtitle: Adults, 2024/25; total-response ethnicity
interpretation: Survey adults are 15+; year labels name July-June survey periods. Barriers can overlap and must not be added. Ribbons/bars are published 95% confidence intervals. Ethnic groups overlap; differences are unadjusted and do not identify causes.

title: New subsidies also cover some existing care
subtitle: GP use and reported free last visits by age, 2024/25
interpretation: GP visit measures past-year contact; free-last-visit uses the indicator's eligible visitor population. Denominators differ; neither gives the number of newly created appointments.

title: Read future health funding alongside unallocated allowances
subtitle: PREFU existing functional baselines
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises. Future new spending is not yet allocated to health; this is not a complete final health budget or productivity measure.

title: Value depends on additional care, not subsidised visits alone
subtitle: Sensitivity grid: extra spending divided by genuinely additional completed appointments
interpretation: Entirely illustrative, not a Medicard costing. No baseline visit substitution, downstream health savings, quality or capacity response has been estimated.

title: There is no single household inflation experience
subtitle: Household living-cost indexes through September 2026
interpretation: Indexes reflect group expenditure baskets, including interest payments. Income groups can change composition; these are not the same households followed over time.

title: Lower inflation does not restore the earlier price level
subtitle: Cumulative cost of maintaining each group's spending basket
interpretation: A cost index is not household wellbeing or disposable income; expenditure weights update over time. Base quarter and endpoint are common across groups.

title: Which costs changed the household budget?
subtitle: Selected group-level price indexes for all households
interpretation: Component price growth is not its contribution to total inflation: expenditure weights differ. Housing/utilities and interest are distinct HLPI groups.

title: Are wage gains restoring purchasing power?
subtitle: Observed wages through June 2026; average earnings versus fixed-quality wage rates
interpretation: QES averages move with workforce composition; LCI controls job quality. Gross hourly wages exclude taxes, transfers, hours changes and non-wage income.

title: The same wage series buys different household baskets
subtitle: National average gross hourly earnings deflated by each group's living costs
interpretation: Benchmark comparison, NOT measured wage growth of beneficiaries, retirees or each income quintile. Shows basket sensitivity, not household disposable-income recovery.

title: Hourly wages are only part of earned income
subtitle: Seasonally adjusted employment and paid-hours context through June 2026
interpretation: Different survey populations: QES paid hours per FTE are not HLFS total hours. Do not multiply these series into a household income estimate.

title: Housing tenure helps explain different cost pressures
subtitle: Latest household-profile benchmark year: 2024
interpretation: Historical survey benchmark, not September 2026 tenure. Other tenure is the residual, not solely private renters. Ownership categories are source household definitions.

title: Tax-rate cuts and investment deductions target different firms
subtitle: Illustrative new $100,000 eligible asset; 20% diminishing-value depreciation
interpretation: 28% standard rate versus proposed 20% SME rate and deduction alternatives. No loss refunds, financing or imputation; profit is before asset deductions. Illustrative, not a party costing.

title: A deduction need not deliver cash to a loss-making firm
subtitle: Same illustrative investment; tax losses are not refunded in this model
interpretation: Carry-forward value depends on future taxable profits and loss rules. This chart measures unused deductions, not their ultimate economic value.

title: Expensing primarily changes the timing of deductions
subtitle: $100,000 asset; full lifetime deductions reconcile to its cost
interpretation: Assumed depreciation rate. Investment Boost deducts 20% at purchase and depreciates the remaining 80%; ordinary depreciation starts at year one. Profits sufficient to use deductions.

title: Compare tax relief in present-value terms
subtitle: Same asset and cash-flow timing, different rates and deductions
interpretation: Assumes deductions can be used immediately when scheduled. Does not measure induced investment, compliance costs or the fiscal cost of a tax change.

title: Which change lowers the hurdle for a new investment?
subtitle: Perpetual unlevered cash-flow model with an immediately usable deduction
interpretation: Zero inflation, no disposal value, no shareholder tax or financing. Full expensing gives zero wedge under these assumptions; this is not an economy-wide empirical estimate.

title: Investment policy needs an outcome benchmark
subtitle: R&D intensity: New Zealand, Australia and the OECD aggregate
interpretation: Descriptive context from the existing snapshot. R&D intensity is not an estimate of tax-credit additionality, and comparator institutions differ.

title: Who performs research and development?
subtitle: Stats NZ published sector observations; available survey years only
interpretation: Spending is nominal; business 2025 and all-sector 2024 coverage differ. Sampling errors and footnotes are retained in the data. No interpolation or causal credit effect is estimated.

title: Track the fiscal input separately from the R&D outcome
subtitle: 2026 tax expenditure statement; published actual/estimate/forecast labels
interpretation: Expense measures support through the tax system, not additional R&D caused by it. Do not divide total R&D by this series and call the ratio a return on the credit.

title: Membership and active saving are different measures
subtitle: IRD contributions through Inland Revenue or reported by providers
interpretation: Includes children, retirees and overseas members. Direct-provider contributions can be incompletely observed. Not the share of employed adults failing to save.

title: Where compulsory saving would start
subtitle: IRD employee contribution-rate classification, June 2026
interpretation: No PAYE contribution includes members saving outside payroll. These are employee rates; employer contributions face ESCT. 3.5% is the current default, 6% is a proposed future rate.

title: Who supplies the recorded retirement contributions?
subtitle: Gross flows to providers through Inland Revenue
interpretation: Excludes voluntary payments directly to providers. Government payments can lag the earning year; these are flows, not balances, net national saving or economic incidence.

title: Not all KiwiSaver saving stays invested until retirement
subtitle: First-home and hardship withdrawals reported to IRD
interpretation: IRD notes provider reporting may be incomplete and these are not all withdrawal types. First-home use buys another asset; it is not necessarily a reduction in household wealth.

title: Retirement lasts an uncertain number of years
subtitle: Stats NZ 2022-2024 period mortality; national median life-table estimates
interpretation: Period tables hold observed mortality rates fixed. They are not a forecast for today's workers; future longevity, health and group differences matter. 105 is an open interval.

title: Planning to an average lifespan leaves longevity risk
subtitle: Equal weights on male/female survivors at 65; period-life-table arithmetic
interpretation: A fixed drawdown plan is not lifetime insurance. No mortality improvement assumed. Unisex weights are illustrative, not actual buyer weights or population forecasts.

title: What capital funds a lifelong real income?
subtitle: $30,000 a year, CPI-level single-life annuity; assumed 5% expense loading
interpretation: Actuarial illustration, not an annuity quote or NZ Super liability valuation. No survivor/refund benefit; period mortality and approximate midyear timing including the 105+ tail.

title: Pooling longevity changes the financing arithmetic
subtitle: 2% real discount; actuarial cost without expense loading in both comparisons
interpretation: The fixed plan pays everyone for the whole chosen horizon and can leave bequests. The annuity stops at death, has no bequest, and relies on a solvent pool. Not equivalent contracts.

title: Compulsory deposits build assets, not a specified pension
subtitle: $70,000 constant real gross earnings; 3% return net of tax and fees
interpretation: Contribution fractions are net amounts invested, not employee-plus-employer headline rates. End-year deposits, no breaks/withdrawals. Not an estimate of additional national saving.

title: Translate retirement balances into income
subtitle: Forty years of contributions; same annuity pricing assumptions across accumulation returns
interpretation: Annuity uses 2% real liability discount, period mortality, 5% loading. Risky accumulation returns do not increase the liability discount. CPI-level payout, not wage-indexed NZ Super.

title: Contribution-based pensions reflect earnings histories
subtitle: $70,000 full-time earnings; 8% invested; 3% net real return; same annuity basis
interpretation: No compensating caregiver credits or government top-ups. Scenarios isolate timing and earnings; they do not estimate actual gender or disability gaps.

title: Annual fees compound into differences in retirement income
subtitle: 8% invested from $70,000 earnings for 40 years; 4% real return after tax, before fees
interpretation: Assumed fee range, not measured KiwiSaver fees. Fees charged proportionally to assets after gross investment return. Same mortality and annuity expense loading throughout.

title: Pre-funding a promised income requires an explicit contribution
subtitle: Target $30,000 CPI-level lifelong income from 65; fixed annuity pricing basis
interpretation: Conditional on survival to 65; no pre-retirement mortality pooling. Required contribution is a net deposit, not a payroll tax or a costing of universal NZ Super. Return risk remains.

title: Individual ownership and a common pension distribute differently
subtitle: Same total deposits from an artificial equal-sized earnings grid; 8% invested for 40 years
interpretation: Common benefit redistributes within this synthetic cohort. Grid is not NZ's earnings distribution. No aggregate saving advantage is assumed; mortality and pricing are identical.

title: Pre-funding requires resources during the transition
subtitle: Extra end-year deposits; 3% net real return; 2% real GDP growth; no withdrawals
interpretation: Existing pensions still need financing. If deposits are debt-funded, gross assets overstate net pre-funding; no borrowing costs, tax changes or pension offsets are included.

title: Who funds higher retirement contributions?
subtitle: Two remuneration assumptions; 30% illustrative ESCT; current income-tax schedule
interpretation: Employer contributions need not be a free addition to lifetime pay. Includes no ACC, government top-up or wage bargaining response. Scenarios bracket assumptions, not measured incidence.

title: Collective pre-funding already has an investment history
subtitle: NZ Super Fund published cumulative indices through its latest saved month
interpretation: Provisional, after costs and before NZ tax. Benchmark risk differs; historical excess returns are not guaranteed or a risk-free financing gain. Index excludes government cash contributions.

title: CPI-level and growing real pensions cost different amounts
subtitle: $30,000 initial annual pension; same mortality and 5% loading
interpretation: 1% real payment growth is a sensitivity, not the statutory NZ Super indexation formula or a wage forecast. Comparing individual balances with public promises requires matching indexation.

title: The public pension promise grows with numbers and payment rates
subtitle: PREFU NZ Super expense and published recipient-count series
interpretation: 2026 fiscal results are unaudited; 2027 onward are forecasts (dashed divider). Policy baseline, not election promises. Recipient statistics and expense flows need consistent timing; ratio is not a statutory payment rate. Individual KiwiSaver balances do not automatically reduce this public obligation.

title: Bigger retirement accounts need not mean equal new saving
subtitle: Illustrative $5 billion increase in account deposits, including any public subsidy
interpretation: Static accounting sensitivity: subtract displaced other saving and additional public dissaving. Not estimated KiwiSaver additionality. Does not model consumption, investment or general-equilibrium responses.
